extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, and scholars of constitutional theory and American founding-era political thought
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating constitutional mechanisms (especially appeals to the people/conventions) intended to check encroachments among the three departments of government and preserve the constitutional equilibrium. Focuses on when popular recourse is appropriate and what structural features a remedy must have to be effective and non‑dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit appeals to the People to 'great and extraordinary occasions'
rubrics_metrics.description: "a constitutional road to the decision of the People ought to be marked out and kept open, for certain great and extraordinary occasions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madison endorses keeping popular recourse available but only for exceptional cases; he argues a formal channel should exist but its use must be restricted to avoid undermining the stability and reverence of government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy must be effective against combinations of departments
rubrics_metrics.description: "the provision does not reach the case of a combination of two of the departments against a third."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A constitutional remedy that requires concurrence of two departments cannot protect a department when two branches collude; effective checks must address coalition scenarios and not be neutralized by combined majorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid frequent appeals — preserve the government’s veneration and stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent appeals to the People would, in a great measure, deprive the Government of that veneration which time bestows on everything, and without which perhaps the wisest and freest Governments would not possess the requisite stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because government legitimacy rests on public opinion, too‑frequent recourse implies persistent defect and erodes respect for institutions; mechanisms should therefore discourage trivial or frequent recourse and be used sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't design remedies that will unduly inflame public passions
rubrics_metrics.description: The danger of disturbing the public tranquillity by interesting too strongly the public passions, is a still more serious objection against a frequent reference of constitutional questions to the decision of the whole society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referenda or conventions risk turning constitutional questions into contests of passion rather than deliberation; designers should avoid procedures that invite emotional, unstable, or partisan mobilization of the public on constitutional matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for asymmetrical advantages among branches (legislative advantage)
rubrics_metrics.description: The members of the Legislative department... are distributed and dwell among the People at large. Their connections of blood, of friendship, and of acquaintance, embrace a great proportion of the most influential part of the society... With these advantages, it can hardly be supposed that the adverse party would have an equal chance for a favorable issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When allowing popular recourse, recognize that the legislature enjoys social and electoral advantages (numbers, local presence, personal ties) that bias outcomes; remedies should not magnify structural advantages of any one branch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent parties from judging their own causes — ensure impartial decision-makers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Convention, in short, would be composed chiefly of men who had been, who actually were, or who expected to be, members of the department whose conduct was arraigned. They would consequently be parties to the very question to be decided by them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection methods for any decision-making body (convention, assembly) must avoid composition dominated by those with direct stakes in the dispute, since that produces partiality and defeats the remedial purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design processes to secure reasoned decisions rather than partisan judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: The passions, therefore, not the reason, of the public, would sit in judgment. But it is the reason of the public alone, that ought to control and regulate the Government. The passions ought to be controlled and regulated by the Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional remedies should favor deliberative, reasoned judgment and include institutional filters that temper popular passion and party zeal so decisions reflect merits rather than factional impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere declarations in the written constitution are insufficient; include structural provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: We found in the last paper, that mere declarations in the written Constitution are not sufficient to restrain the several departments within their legal rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond textual assertions of powers and limits, designers must craft practical structural provisions (checks, balances, selection rules, insulating mechanisms) to restrain departments and preserve equilibrium; some such provisions may be "founded on sound political principles."
